locator.text: Display 60.5, p. 60, in the proof of Proposition 5.5

evidence: paper: \big[(q\partial_q)^j \chi(c_n q)\big] = \big[(\sigma\partial_\sigma)^j \chi(\sigma)\big]\Big|_{\sigma = c_n q}, \qquad \sup_{n\ge 1,\; q>0} \big|(q\partial_q)^j \chi(c_n q)\big| \;\le\; \sup_{\sigma>0} \big|(\sigma\partial_\sigma)^j \chi(\sigma)\big| \;=:\; C_j \;<\; \infty .

provenance.note: machine audit: worker, gate, reviewer; not confirmed by a human

verdicts.summary: Lean has an equivalent formula. Same content, written with the plain derivative instead of the Euler operator. The paper's first identity is the scale invariance of (q∂_q)^j under q ↦ c_n q; Lean states the equivalent chain rule ∂_q^n(χ(a·)) (q) = a^n (∂^n χ)(aq) (scaledCutoff_iteratedDeriv). The paper's uniform-in-n bound C_j is Lean's existential C in scaledCutoff_iteratedDeriv_bound / cutoff_jet_bound: the constant is quantified before the scale a, so it is independent of a (hence of n), which is exactly 'sup over n ≥ 1, q > 0'. The rewriting between the two forms: (q∂_q)^j = Σ_{k≤j} S(j,k) q^k ∂_q^k with Stirling numbers S(j,k), so |(q∂_q)^j χ(c_n q)| ≤ Σ_k S(j,k) q^k · c_n^k |χ^{(k)}(c_n q)|, and Lean's q^{-k} bound on ∂_q^k times q^k gives a finite a-independent constant; conversely Lean's q^{-m} form follows from the paper's C_j by q^m ∂_q^m = Σ_k s(m,k)(q∂_q)^k. Lean also quantifies over every real scale a ≥ 0 rather than the sequence c_n, which is a strictly larger supremum, and states the bound for q > 0 on a set S (cutoff_jet_bound) rather than all q > 0.
